pages.title: How to Develop an Answer
pages.description: The point-evidence-explanation-effect-link structure behind every good Literature answer, shown step by step from a one-line response to a full paragraph.
pages.keywords: developing an answer, PEE, point evidence explanation, literature essay paragraph

hero.text: Most students know the answer. What they lose marks for is stopping after the first sentence of it. This page is about the four sentences that follow.

blocks.heading: The problem, exactly
text: A student is asked how a writer presents a character. They write: *The writer shows that he is proud.* That is correct. It earns very little.

The marks are not for knowing that he is proud. They are for showing **where** the text says so, **how** the writing conveys it, and **what difference** it makes. Those are three separate things, and each has to be written down.

blocks.heading: The five parts of a developed answer

items.title: Point
text: Answer the question in one sentence. Not an introduction — the actual answer. *The writer presents him as a man whose pride is stronger than his judgement.*

items.title: Evidence
text: Give the proof: a short quotation, or a precise reference to a moment. Keep quotations short — a few words is usually enough, and long quotations waste examination time.

items.title: Explanation
text: Explain how the evidence supports the point. Look at the actual words: a particular verb, an image, a repetition, a silence.

items.title: Effect
text: Say what it does to the reader or the audience. This is the sentence weak answers never contain, and it is where the higher marks live.

items.title: Link
text: Connect it to the question, or to the wider text. One sentence: how this contributes to the theme, the character's development, or the writer's purpose.

blocks.heading: The same answer, developed four times
intro: The example is invented for illustration, so that the method can be shown without quoting a copyrighted text. Watch the answer grow.

items.label: Stage 1 — Point only (very few marks)
items.prompt: How does the writer present the father in this extract?
sample: The writer presents the father as a proud man.
notes: Correct, and almost worthless. There is no evidence and no explanation. An examiner cannot tell whether the student has read the text or guessed.

items.label: Stage 2 — Point and evidence
items.prompt: How does the writer present the father in this extract?
sample: The writer presents the father as a proud man. When his son offers him money, he says, "I have managed thirty years without it."
notes: Better. There is now proof. But the quotation has been left to speak for itself, and it does not — the student has not said what in it shows pride.

items.label: Stage 3 — Point, evidence and explanation
items.prompt: How does the writer present the father in this extract?
sample: The writer presents the father as a proud man. When his son offers him money, he says, "I have managed thirty years without it." The reply does not refuse the money directly; instead it turns the offer into a comment on his own endurance, and the precise figure of "thirty years" suggests a man who has been counting.
notes: Now the words themselves are being examined — the indirect refusal, and the exactness of *thirty years*. This is the level most students can reach with practice, and it earns solid marks.

items.label: Stage 4 — All five parts (full marks available)
items.prompt: How does the writer present the father in this extract?
sample: The writer presents the father as a proud man whose pride has become a way of keeping his son at a distance. When the son offers him money, he says, "I have managed thirty years without it." The reply does not refuse the money directly; instead it turns the offer into a comment on his own endurance, and the precise figure of "thirty years" suggests a man who has been counting, and who has waited for the chance to say so. The effect on the reader is uncomfortable rather than admiring: we recognise the dignity, but we also see that the son has been refused something more than money. This prepares us for the silence between them in the final scene, which the writer never explains and never needs to.
notes: **Point** — the opening sentence answers the question, and answers it with an argument (*pride has become a way of keeping his son at a distance*), not merely a label.
**Evidence** — one short quotation. Nine words.
**Explanation** — the actual language is examined: the indirectness, the precision of the number.
**Effect** — *uncomfortable rather than admiring* tells the examiner what the writing does to a reader. This sentence is the difference between a good answer and a very good one.
**Link** — the final sentence connects the moment to the rest of the text.
The whole paragraph is five sentences. It is not long. Length is not what is being rewarded — development is.

blocks.heading: Sentence starters for each part
text: Use these while you are learning the structure. Stop using them once the structure has become a habit — an answer built entirely of formulas reads mechanically.

parts.heading: Point
bullets: The writer presents…
The poet suggests that…
At this moment the play shows…

parts.heading: Evidence
bullets: This is shown when…
The phrase "…" indicates…
When she refuses to…

parts.heading: Explanation
bullets: The word "…" implies…
By choosing to… rather than…, the writer…
The repetition of "…" emphasises…

parts.heading: Effect
bullets: The effect on the reader is…
This makes the audience feel…
We are therefore led to…

parts.heading: Link
bullets: This prepares us for…
The same idea returns when…
This contributes to the theme of…

blocks.title: A practice exercise that works
text: Take any one-sentence answer you have written before and rewrite it as five sentences, one for each part. Do this three times a week for a fortnight.
It is dull, and it is the single most reliable way to raise a Literature mark, because the failure to develop is almost always the reason the mark was low.

pages.title: Context Questions
pages.description: How to answer O/L Literature context questions on a printed extract: what each kind of question wants, how long each answer should be, and the errors that waste time.
pages.keywords: context questions, extract questions, O/L Literature, short answers

hero.text: Context answers should be short. Students lose more marks here by writing too much than by writing too little.

blocks.heading: What a context question is
text: A short extract from a text you have studied is printed, followed by several short questions. They test whether you can **place** the extract, **understand** what is happening at that moment, and **comment** briefly on the language.
The marks per question are small. Match your answer to the marks, and move on.

blocks.heading: The kinds of context question, and what each wants
rows: Who is speaking, and to whom?
The names, and their relationship if it is relevant
One sentence
Where does this occur in the text?
The stage of the story, not the page number
One sentence
What has just happened?
The immediately preceding event, not a summary of the book
One or two sentences
What does the speaker mean?
The meaning in plain words, in this situation
One or two sentences
Explain the underlined phrase
The literal meaning plus what it suggests here
Two sentences
What does this reveal about the character?
A quality, plus the words that show it
Two or three sentences
Identify the technique and its effect
Name it, quote it, say what it does
Two or three sentences
What happens next?
The immediate consequence, briefly
One or two sentences

blocks.heading: The method
numbered: **Read the whole extract before any question.** Place it in the text in your own mind first.
**Read all the questions before answering.** They often move in order through the extract, and a later question sometimes tells you how to read an earlier one.
**Look at the marks.** One mark is one point. Three marks is three points, or one point developed.
**Answer only what is asked.** Extra material cannot gain marks, can contradict you, and costs time.
**Quote from the extract, not from memory.** The extract is printed in front of you. Use it, and copy it exactly.
**Answer in complete sentences** unless a single word is clearly what is wanted.

blocks.heading: Short answers, correctly judged
intro: The extract referred to is invented for illustration. Watch how short a full-mark answer can be.

items.label: One-mark question
items.prompt: Who is speaking these words, and to whom? (1 mark)
sample: The father is speaking to his son.
notes: One mark, one sentence. Anything more is wasted time. Some students write a paragraph here and then run short at the three-mark question below.

items.label: Two-mark question
items.prompt: What has just happened before this moment? (2 marks)
sample: The son has returned home after several years away and has offered his father money. The father has not yet spoken since he entered the house.
notes: Two marks, two facts, two clauses. The answer stays in the immediate context and does not summarise the whole story.

items.label: Three-mark question
items.prompt: What does the phrase "thirty years" suggest about the father? (3 marks)
sample: It suggests that he has been counting the years of his own struggle, and has been waiting for an opportunity to say so.
The precision of the figure makes the remark sound rehearsed, which implies long-held resentment rather than a reply made on the spur of the moment.
It therefore reveals a pride that has hardened over time into a grievance.
notes: Three marks, three developed points, each in its own sentence.
Notice that the answer moves from what the words say, to what they imply, to what they reveal — the same movement as point, explanation, effect, compressed.
It is still short. Three sentences is a complete three-mark answer.

blocks.heading: Habits that gain and lose marks
do: Match the length of the answer to the marks.
Quote from the printed extract, exactly.
Answer in your own words where explanation is asked for.
Number your answers to match the paper.
dont: Summarise the whole text when asked what has just happened.
Write a paragraph for a one-mark question.
Copy long stretches of the extract instead of explaining.
Give two alternative answers and hope one is right — the examiner may mark the first.
Leave the last question because time ran out on the first.

pages.title: Essay Questions
pages.description: How to read, plan and write an O/L Literature essay: understanding the question, choosing evidence, structuring paragraphs and reaching a real conclusion.
pages.keywords: literature essay, essay questions, O/L Literature, planning, argument, evidence

hero.text: A Literature essay is an argument supported by evidence. It is not a retelling, and it is not everything you know about the text.

items.title: Find the instruction word
text: *Discuss*, *examine*, *how far do you agree*, *show how*, *compare*, *what is the significance of*. Each demands a different shape. *How far do you agree* requires you to take a position and to consider the other side; *show how* requires method rather than opinion.

items.title: Find the subject
text: Is the question about a character, a theme, a relationship, a technique or a moment? Underline it. Then check every paragraph you write against it.

items.title: Notice the limits
text: *In the first half*, *in the opening scene*, *in this poem*. A question limited to part of a text becomes wrong when answered from the whole of it.

items.title: Rewrite the question as a statement
text: *How far do you agree that the father's pride destroys his family?* becomes *The father's pride destroys his family — to this extent.* Now you can see what you have to argue.

blocks.heading: Planning: five minutes, well spent
text: Do not write an essay plan in sentences. Write it like this, in five lines.
numbered: **My answer in one sentence** — this becomes the last sentence of your introduction.
**Paragraph 1 idea + evidence** — a point, and the moment in the text that proves it.
**Paragraph 2 idea + evidence** — a different point, not the same one restated.
**Paragraph 3 idea + evidence** — often the complication, the opposing view, or the development late in the text.
**Conclusion** — the judgement you will reach, decided **before** you begin writing.

text: That plan takes four or five minutes and prevents the two commonest disasters: an essay with no argument, and an essay that stops because the time ran out rather than because it had finished.

parts.heading: Introduction (three or four sentences)
text: Name the text and the writer. Address the question directly. End with your position. Do **not** write a biography of the author, and do not begin *In this essay I am going to…*

parts.heading: Body paragraphs (three or four)
text: Each one point, developed using [point, evidence, explanation, effect, link](ol-literature/developing-an-answer/). Each should begin with the point, not with an event.

parts.heading: The paragraph that raises the other side
text: For *how far do you agree* questions, one paragraph should consider the opposite case honestly and then answer it. An essay that ignores the obvious counter-argument looks as though it has not noticed it.

parts.heading: Conclusion (three or four sentences)
text: Answer the question. Not a summary of your paragraphs — a judgement. It should be possible for a reader to tell from your conclusion alone what you actually think.

blocks.heading: An introduction and a conclusion, compared

items.label: Weak and strong introductions
items.prompt: How far do you agree that the father's pride is the cause of the family's suffering?
sample: **Weak:** In this essay I am going to discuss the father's pride. The father is a very important character in this story. There are many things to say about him. First I will discuss his character.

**Strong:** The father's pride is the most visible cause of the family's suffering, but it is not, in the end, the deepest one. The writer shows a man whose refusal of help is real and damaging, yet also shows the poverty and the loss of work that made such a refusal feel necessary to him. Pride is therefore better understood as the form his suffering takes than as its origin.
notes: The weak introduction announces; it does not argue. It could have been written without reading the text.

The strong introduction takes a position in its first sentence and immediately qualifies it — *but it is not, in the end, the deepest one*. A qualified position is what *how far do you agree* is asking for.
It also, in three sentences, tells the examiner what the whole essay will argue. That is what an introduction is for.

blocks.heading: Checklist for a Literature essay
items: Have I answered the **question set**, and not a similar question I had prepared?
Does every paragraph **begin with a point**, not with an event?
Does every paragraph contain **evidence** — a short quotation or a precise reference?
Have I explained **how** the writing works, not only what it says?
Have I said what the **effect** on the reader or audience is?
Have I considered the **other side**, where the question invites it?
Does my conclusion give a **judgement**, not a summary?
Have I named the writer and used the **present tense** for what happens in the text?

pages.title: Model Answers
pages.metaTitle: O/L Literature Model Answers: Context and Essay, Marking Scheme Format | RCF English
pages.description: O/L Appreciation of English Literary Texts model answers in the real paper format: four-part context answers, the Section B novel extract, and 15-mark essays on all four genres.
pages.keywords: O/L literature model answers, appreciation of English literary texts, context question format, section B novel extract, O/L literature essay answers

hero.text: Eight model answers - one context and one essay for each of poetry, prose, drama and the novel - written to the mark allocations the paper actually uses.

blocks.title: Read this first
bullets: **The question formats and mark splits on this page are taken from real papers**, checked against the G.C.E. O/L *Appreciation of English Literary Texts* government paper and marking scheme.
The **answers** are written by RCF English. They are not official answers and not the only acceptable ones.
**Do not memorise them.** Marking schemes accept several wordings; what they do not accept is an answer that does not fit the question asked.
Quotations are from texts that are **out of copyright**. Prescribed texts change, so check your own year's syllabus.

blocks.heading: Paper I: what you are actually asked
blocks.caption: Structure taken from the government paper. Paper I carries 40 marks; 10 minutes additional reading time is given before the three hours begin.
rows: **Section A - Poetry**
Two extracts. **Answer all.**
**Section A - Prose**
Two extracts. **Answer all.**
**Section A - Drama**
Two extracts. **Answer all.**
**Section B - Novels**
One longer extract. **Select EITHER (1), (2) OR (3)** and answer all the questions under it.
**Paper I total**
Section A is compulsory in full; only Section B offers a choice.

blocks.heading: The two question shapes, and their exact mark splits
blocks.caption: Learn these two shapes and you know in advance how long every answer must be.
rows: Part (a) / (i)
**1 mark** - Name the poem / work / play. Name the poet / author / writer.
**2 marks** - When and where does the incident take place?
Part (b) / (ii)
**1 mark** - Who is referred to as 'he' / 'they' / 'you'? Or: to whom is it spoken?
**2 marks** - Briefly describe the speaker's emotions.
Part (c) / (iii)
**1 mark** - Name a literary device / when is it said / what is meant by a phrase.
**1 + 1 mark** - Explain the meaning of two phrases as used in the extract.
Part (d) / (iv)
**2 marks** - Theme, significance, character or emotions.
**4 marks** - Comment briefly on the significant theme or themes.
**Total**

blocks.title: The three rules that follow from those mark splits
text: **One mark means a few words.** Parts (a), (b) and (c) are worth one mark each. The answer is a name, a person, or a device - not a sentence explaining your reasoning. Six context questions, three one-mark parts each: eighteen of your forty marks are won or lost in single phrases.
**Two marks means two things.** Part (d) is worth two, so give two ideas, or one idea plus its support. A single word will not earn two marks; a paragraph will not earn three.

**Four marks means the only place you write at length.** Part (iv) of the Section B extract is the one part of Paper I that wants developed comment. Name more than one theme and tie each to the passage.
Answer the six Section A extracts in about **eight minutes each**, and leave twenty minutes for Section B.

items.label: 5 marks: 1 + 1 + 1 + 2
items.prompt:
"He stirred his velvet head / Like one in danger, cautious"
(a) Name the poem from which these lines are taken. Name the poet. (01 mark)
(b) Who is referred to as 'He' in these lines? (01 mark)
(c) Name a literary device used in these lines. (01 mark)
(d) Why does the speaker assume that 'He' is cautious? (02 marks)
sample: **(a)** *A Bird Came Down the Walk.* Emily Dickinson. **(1)**
**(c)** Simile - *like one in danger*. (*Metaphor* - "velvet head" - is also acceptable.) **(1)**

**(d)** The bird moves its head quickly and watchfully, the way a creature behaves when it senses a threat; and the speaker, who is watching it closely, is the danger it senses. Its caution shows it is aware of being observed. **(2)**
notes: **(a) is two names.** Nothing else earns anything. Write the poem, write the poet, move on.
**(b) is two words.** *The bird.* Candidates who write *He refers to the bird which the speaker sees walking down the path* get the same one mark and lose thirty seconds.

**(c) asks you to NAME a device, not to explain it.** One mark. Give the name and, if you have room, the two or three words it applies to. Giving a second device is harmless and useful insurance if the first is wrong.

**(d) is worth two, so it has two parts:** what the bird does, and why the speaker reads it as caution. Notice the answer connects the caution to the observer - that is the inference the two marks are for.
**Total: about fifty words for five marks.** That is the correct size.

items.label: 5 marks: 1 + 1 + 1 + 2
items.prompt:
"...but for some days past he had practised with the key of the schoolroom door... he did not believe in trusting too much to luck and accident"
(a) From which work are these lines taken? Name the author. (01 mark)
(b) Who is referred to as 'he' in these lines? (01 mark)
(c) What characteristics are expressed about 'he' in these lines? (01 mark)
(d) Briefly explain the significance of these lines to the prose from which they are taken. (02 marks)
sample: **(a)** *The Lumber Room.* Saki (H. H. Munro). **(1)**
**(c)** He is careful, patient and calculating; he plans ahead. **(1)**

**(d)** The lines show that Nicholas's entry into the lumber room is not a lucky accident but the result of days of preparation. This is significant because it explains how a small boy is able to outwit his aunt throughout the story: his success comes from planning, not from chance, and the whole plot depends on it. **(2)**
notes: **(a) - give the author's pen name and real name if you know both.** *Saki* alone is accepted; *Saki (H. H. Munro)* is safer.
**(c) asks for characteristics - so give adjectives.** Three short ones earn the mark more reliably than one, because the scheme lists several acceptable words and you only need to hit one.
**(d) is the two-mark part, and 'significance' means 'why it matters to the whole story'** - not what the lines say. An answer that paraphrases the quotation scores nothing here.
The two marks are earned by two moves: **what the detail shows** (preparation, not luck) and **why that matters** (it explains how he beats the aunt).

items.label: 5 marks: 1 + 1 + 1 + 2
items.prompt:
"I've locked myself in, and will be true to you till the grave, and you... aren't you ashamed, you bad child?"
(a) Name the play from which these lines are taken. Name the writer. (01 mark)
(b) To whom does the speaker say these lines? (01 mark)
(c) What is meant by "I've locked myself in"? (01 mark)
(d) Briefly describe the speaker's character as presented in these lines. (02 marks)
sample: **(a)** *The Bear.* Anton Chekhov. **(1)**
**(b)** To her dead husband, Nicolai Mihailovitch, whose portrait she is addressing. **(1)**
**(c)** That she has shut herself away from society and refuses to leave the house or see anyone since her husband's death. **(1)**

**(d)** Popova is presented as dramatic and self-consciously devoted, making a public performance of her mourning; and at the same time reproachful and self-righteous, since she scolds her dead husband for his unfaithfulness even while vowing to be true to him. The contradiction makes her faithfulness look more like pride than grief. **(2)**
notes: **(b) is the trap in drama extracts.** The words are spoken aloud, but not to another living character. Candidates who answer *to Luka* or *to Smirnov* lose an easy mark.
**(c) asks what a phrase means, not what it symbolises.** Give the literal sense - she has shut herself indoors - in one sentence.
**(d) is worth two, so give two qualities that pull against each other.** *Devoted* on its own is thin; *devoted yet reproachful* shows you have read the line rather than remembered the character.
In *The Bear*, almost every extract rewards noticing the gap between what Popova says and what she does. Look for it.

blocks.heading: Context 4 - Section B, the novel extract

items.label: 10 marks: 2 + 2 + (1 + 1) + 4
items.prompt:
From *The Prince and the Pauper*: the Recognition Procession, in which Tom Canty, riding as king, sees his mother in the crowd, denies her, and is then overwhelmed with shame.
(i) When and where does the incident take place? (02 marks)
(ii) Briefly describe the speaker's emotions presented in the passage. (02 marks)
(iii) Explain the meaning of these phrases as used in the extract: (a) "his senses swam in a delirium of pleasure" (01 mark) (b) "withered his stolen royalty" (01 mark)
(iv) Comment briefly on the significant theme or themes represented in the passage. (04 marks)
sample: **(i)** During the Recognition Procession through the City of London, on the day before the coronation, while Tom Canty is riding through the streets as king. **(2)**

**(ii)** At first he is excited, proud and intoxicated by the crowd's attention. When he recognises his mother he feels shock and panic, and after the guard strikes her away he feels shame, guilt and worthlessness, so that his grandeur means nothing to him. **(2)**
**(iii) (a)** He was dizzy with delight; the excitement was so great that he could hardly think clearly. **(1)**
**(iii) (b)** His royal position, which was not truly his, lost all its value and pride in that moment. **(1)**
**(iv)** Several themes come together here.
**Appearance and reality:** Tom wears the outward show of kingship but is not a king, and the passage strips the show away in an instant.
**Identity:** the involuntary gesture of his hand betrays who he really is, showing that identity cannot be put on and off with clothing.
**Guilt and conscience:** his denial of his mother is the moral centre of the passage, and his shame shows that his conscience is not corrupted by his new position.
**Class and power:** the officer's casual violence towards a poor woman shows how the powerless are treated, and Tom, who has just come from that class, can do nothing to stop it. **(4)**
notes: **(i) asks for two things - when AND where - so give both.** Two marks, two pieces of information. *In London* alone is half an answer.
**(ii) is a sequence, not a single feeling.** The emotions change inside the passage: pride, then shock, then shame. Tracking the change is what earns both marks.
**(iii) tests whether you can put an image into plain English.** Do not repeat the phrase and do not analyse it. *Delirium of pleasure* becomes *dizzy with delight*. One mark each, one sentence each.

**(iv) is worth four marks and is the only part of Paper I where you write at length.** Name several themes, label them, and attach each to something in the passage. Four separate labelled points is the safest shape - it is easy to mark and hard to miss.
**Do not retell the extract.** The examiner has just read it. Every sentence must add a theme or explain one.

blocks.heading: Paper II: the essay questions
text: Paper II is answered in a separate booklet. You answer **one essay from each genre section** - Poetry, Drama, Prose and Fiction - each worth **15 marks**.

The marking scheme for these does not print a model essay. It prints a **list of indicative points**, and then says that candidates are expected to provide **textual evidence** for them, and that an answer arguing the opposite case is equally acceptable if it is supported. That tells you exactly what an answer needs: a position, several developed points, and evidence for each.

items.label: 15 marks
items.prompt: Discuss Emily Dickinson's *A Bird Came Down the Walk* as a minute observation of nature.
sample: Dickinson's poem is built almost entirely out of close watching. The speaker does not tell us that nature is beautiful; she records exactly what one bird does over the space of a minute, and the beauty and the strangeness both come out of the accuracy of that record.

The observation begins with something most poets would leave out. The bird "bit an Angleworm in halves / And ate the fellow, raw". This is not a decorative image of nature but a small act of violence, noticed and reported without comment. By refusing to soften it, Dickinson establishes that she is watching rather than admiring.

The detail then becomes finer still. The bird drinks "a Dew / From a convenient Grass", hops sideways to let a beetle pass, and glances about with eyes that "looked like frightened Beads". Each of these is something that can only be seen by someone standing very still and very close. The simile of the beads is exact: it captures the roundness, the hardness and the quick shine of a bird's eye in three words.

The description also gives the bird a character. It is cautious - it "stirred his velvet head / Like one in danger" - and it is self-possessed, refusing the crumb the speaker offers and leaving on its own terms. Dickinson observes behaviour closely enough to infer a temperament from it, which is what raises the poem above simple description.

The final stanza changes the scale without breaking the method. The bird's flight is compared to oars dividing the ocean and to butterflies leaping "off Banks of Noon", and the movement becomes silent, smooth and enormous. The observation has not stopped; it has simply followed the bird out of the small world of the garden path into the air.

The poem is therefore a minute observation in both senses of the word: it covers about a minute of a bird's life, and it records that minute in very small detail. What Dickinson demonstrates is that close attention is itself a way of understanding nature - the bird is never explained, only watched, and the watching is enough.
notes: **It answers the exact wording.** The question says *minute observation*, and the essay keeps returning to the closeness of the watching rather than writing generally about nature poetry.
**Quotations are short and frequent** - five of them, none longer than a line. The scheme requires textual evidence, and short quotations let you use more of them.
**Each paragraph makes one point and develops it:** the unsoftened violence, the fineness of detail, the inferred character, the change of scale.
**The last paragraph does something extra.** It picks up the double meaning of *minute* - the question's own word - which is the kind of touch that separates a good answer from a routine one.
**About 400 words, six short paragraphs.** You have four of these to write, so this is the realistic size.

items.label: 15 marks
items.prompt: In *The Lumber Room*, despite ill-treatment, Nicholas remains happy. Support your answer with examples from the text.
sample: Nicholas is happy throughout the story, and he is happy because he is never really the victim his aunt believes him to be. She designs a punishment for him; he uses it as the opportunity he had been waiting for.

The ill-treatment is real enough. The aunt excludes him from the trip to Jagborough as a punishment for the affair of the frog in his bread-and-milk, forbids him the gooseberry garden, and appoints herself its guard for the afternoon. Her purpose is that he should feel shut out while the other children enjoy themselves.

But Nicholas has prepared. He had "practised with the key of the schoolroom door" for some days, because he "did not believe in trusting too much to luck and accident". He then pretends to want the gooseberry garden, knowing the aunt will post herself there, and so draws her out of the house. His punishment is what frees him, and he has arranged it himself.

His happiness inside the lumber room is genuine rather than merely triumphant. The tapestry of the huntsman and the stag absorbs him completely: he wonders whether the four wolves will attack the man or the stag, and constructs the rest of the story for himself. It is his imagination, not his victory over his aunt, that makes the afternoon a pleasure.

When the aunt falls into the rain-water tank, he finishes the business calmly. He refuses to fetch the ladder on the ground that she herself had forbidden him the garden, and tells her that the Evil One is speaking, since he was taught she would never tell him an untruth. He is not punished for any of it.

The contrast at tea makes the point. Nicholas sits silent, still thinking about the huntsman and the stag, while the aunt sits in "frozen muteness". He remains happy because he possesses two things she does not: a plan, and an imagination that can make a locked and dusty room the most interesting place in the house.
notes: **It agrees with the statement and explains the mechanism.** The question offers a proposition; a good answer says why it is true, not merely that it is.
**Six specific references** - the frog, Jagborough, the practised key, the tapestry, the rain-water tank, the tea table. The scheme asks for textual evidence and this is what that means.
**Two quotations only, both short.** At O/L you do not need many, but you do need the right ones.
**The plot appears only as evidence.** There is no retelling. This is the commonest reason good candidates score in the middle band.
**Present tense throughout**, and the final sentence answers the question directly rather than summarising the paragraphs.

items.label: 15 marks
items.prompt: Both Smirnov and Popova in *The Bear* have similar characteristics. Do you agree? Support your answer with detailed reference to the play.
sample: I agree. Chekhov sets Smirnov and Popova against each other as opposites - a rude creditor and a grieving widow - but the comedy depends on the audience gradually seeing how alike they are, and the ending only works because they are.

Both are theatrical about their own feelings. Popova announces that she has shut herself in and will be true to her husband "till the grave", and says so to his portrait, with the servant listening. Smirnov announces his own woes just as loudly, declaring how many women have wronged him and how he has finished with them for ever. Neither is content to feel something privately.

Both are also proud to the point of absurdity. Popova will not receive a visitor because it would break the performance of her mourning; Smirnov will not leave without his money because leaving would look like a defeat. The whole quarrel continues past the point of sense because neither will be the first to give way.

Their tempers are the clearest similarity. Popova, who has spent the play presenting herself as broken and gentle, accepts the challenge to a duel without hesitation and demands pistols; the woman who could not bear to see anyone is suddenly ready to shoot a stranger in her own garden. Smirnov's admiration at that moment - he calls her a woman he can respect - is the first honest thing either of them says.

Both, finally, change their declared positions completely within a single scene. Popova has sworn lifelong fidelity to a dead husband who, as she herself admits, was unfaithful to her; Smirnov has sworn never to fall in love again. Within minutes of the duel both vows are abandoned, and the speed of the reversal shows that neither belief was as fixed as its owner claimed.

The similarity is therefore the point of the play. Two people who insist loudly on incompatible principles turn out to share the same temperament - impulsive, proud, and more interested in the drama of their own feelings than in the feelings themselves - and it is precisely this likeness that makes the ending believable rather than absurd.
notes: **The question says *do you agree*, so the first word of the answer is a position.** An essay that lists similarities without ever agreeing has not answered.
**Each paragraph takes one shared characteristic** - theatricality, pride, temper, changeability - and shows it in both characters. Never write about one character and then the other.
**The marking scheme accepts a refutation too**, provided evidence is given. If you argue that they are different, you must support it as fully as this supports the agreement.
**The last paragraph explains why the similarity matters** to the play as a whole. Fifteen-mark answers that end with a judgement rather than a summary read as complete.

items.label: 15 marks
items.prompt: What challenges do Edward Tudor and Tom Canty face in *The Prince and the Pauper* when they change their identities? Support your answer with examples from the text.
sample: When the two boys exchange clothes they discover that identity is not simply a matter of appearance, and each faces a different kind of difficulty: Tom must learn to perform a role he does not understand, while Edward must survive in a world that will not believe him.

Tom's first challenge is ignorance of court custom. He does not know the ceremonies of the dining table, the order of precedence, or how to behave towards courtiers and servants, and every small mistake risks exposure. He is also frightened of being discovered and punished as an impostor, so he must conceal his terror while appearing to command.

His deeper challenge is moral rather than practical. He is asked to judge the accused - among them a woman and her daughters condemned to burn - and must decide questions of life and death with no training and no authority he believes in. His success in saving them shows a natural justice that the court has lost, but it costs him great fear.

Tom's hardest moment, however, is personal. When his mother recognises him in the Recognition Procession, he denies her: "I do not know you, woman!" The shame that follows withers what the narrator calls his "stolen royalty", and shows that the challenge of a false identity is not only being found out but what one becomes while keeping it up.

Edward's challenges are physical and constant. He is beaten by John Canty, forced among robbers and beggars, made to endure the hermit who intends to kill him, and treated cruelly at Hendon Hall and in prison. Above all, nobody believes him: the more insistently he declares himself king, the madder he appears, and his rank becomes the very reason he is mocked.

Yet his ordeal is also his education. Because no one takes him for a prince, he sees the cruelty of the law, the treatment of the poor and the conditions of the prisons as no king could otherwise have seen them, and it is this knowledge that later makes him a merciful ruler.

The challenges therefore mirror each other. Tom must learn to be believed when he is not the king; Edward must be disbelieved although he is. Both find that identity depends far more on what others are willing to accept than on what a person truly is - and both are changed by the discovery.
notes: **The question asks about both characters, so the essay is organised in two halves with a linking conclusion.** Answering only about Edward, or only about Tom, halves the marks available.
**Within each half the challenges are ranked** - practical, then moral, then personal for Tom; physical, then the disbelief, then the education for Edward. Ranking shows control of the material.

**Concrete examples throughout:** the dining table, the condemned women, the Recognition Procession, John Canty, the hermit, Hendon Hall, the prison. The scheme lists points of exactly this kind and expects them to be evidenced.
**The conclusion finds the pattern** rather than repeating the list: the two experiences are inversions of each other. That single observation is worth more than another paragraph of examples.

blocks.heading: Common pitfalls
do: Label every part exactly as the paper does: (a), (b), (c), (d) or (i) to (iv).
Give the number of points the marks ask for - one mark, one phrase; two marks, two ideas.
Name both the work and the writer in the identification part, every time.
Answer all six Section A extracts - Section A has no choice in it.
Choose your Section B novel before you start writing, and read all its parts first.
dont: Write a paragraph for a one-mark part. Eighteen of Paper I's forty marks are one-mark parts.
Repeat the words of the extract when asked to explain a phrase in your own words.
Retell the story in a 15-mark essay - the examiner knows it.
Answer two questions from one genre section in Paper II and none from another.
Leave any part blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so a guess costs nothing.

blocks.heading: Language tips
text: Marking schemes for this subject accept several wordings, but they cannot give marks for an answer they cannot follow. These habits cost nothing and protect marks.
bullets: **Write about the text in the present tense.** *Nicholas hides in the lumber room*, not *hid*. Slipping between tenses is the commonest language fault in Literature scripts.
**Name characters and works exactly.** *Popova*, not *the woman*; *The Bear*, not *the drama we studied*. Underline or italicise titles if you can.
**Use short quotations, and put them in quotation marks.** Three or four words is usually enough, and a short accurate quotation is worth far more than a long approximate one.
**Do not begin an essay with a definition.** *Literature is a mirror of society* earns nothing. Begin with your position on the question asked.
**Avoid absolute claims you cannot support** - *everyone agrees*, *this proves*. *This suggests* and *this shows* are safer and just as strong.
**Keep sentences short when the idea is complicated.** A clear simple sentence always outscores a tangled long one.

blocks.heading: Organisation tips
numbered: **Use the ten minutes of additional reading time properly.** Read the whole paper, choose your Section B extract, and decide which essay you will answer in each genre before the three hours begin.
**Do Section A first and fast.** Six extracts at about eight minutes each leaves twenty minutes for Section B and protects the essay time.
**Plan each essay in two minutes.** Three or four points, each with the example you will use. An essay planned in two minutes is written in twenty; an unplanned one takes thirty and repeats itself.
**One idea to a paragraph.** Start with the point, then the example, then what it shows. Four such paragraphs plus an opening position and a closing judgement is a complete 15-mark answer.
**Keep to the same order as the paper** so the examiner can find your answers, and number them clearly.
**Leave five minutes at the end** to check tenses, titles and names - the cheapest marks on the paper.

pages.title: How Teachers Can Mark Answers
pages.description: A practical approach for teachers marking O/L Literature answers, so that a student learns from the mark: what to look for, how to comment, and how to set the next step.
pages.keywords: marking literature answers, teacher marking, feedback, assessment, O/L Literature

hero.text: A mark tells a student where they are. A comment tells them what to do next. Only the second one improves anything.

blocks.heading: The problem with most marking
text: A script comes back covered in red, with *Develop!*, *Explain more*, *Vague* and a mark out of twenty. The student reads the mark, looks at the red, feels defeated, and learns nothing.

The difficulty is not that the comments are wrong. It is that they describe a fault without describing a remedy. *Develop* tells a student that something is missing; it does not tell them what to write instead.

items.title: Read the whole answer once without a pen
text: Decide what the student was trying to argue before you begin correcting. Marking sentence by sentence produces comments on sentences and no comment on the answer.

items.title: Mark the strongest sentence in the answer
text: Underline it and write **"This."** Students rarely know which of their own sentences was the good one. Showing them is the fastest way to get more of the same.

items.title: Choose one fault, not all of them
text: A script with eleven corrections produces no change. A script with one, clearly explained, usually does. Choose the fault that is costing the most marks.

items.title: Write the remedy as an instruction, not a diagnosis
text: Not *needs development*, but: **"After each quotation, add one sentence beginning 'The effect on the reader is…'"** A student can act on that tomorrow.

items.title: Give the mark, and say what would raise it by two
text: **"14. To reach 16, begin each paragraph with a point rather than with an event."** The specific next step matters more than the number.

items.title: Require a rewrite of one paragraph only
text: Not the whole essay. One paragraph, rewritten properly, teaches more than a second full essay marked the same way.

blocks.heading: What to look for, in order of importance
rows: Answering the question
Does every paragraph relate to the question set?
This costs the most marks of anything. Address it first.
Argument
Is there a position, or only a description?
Ask the student to write their answer as one sentence, then use it as the introduction's last line.
Evidence
Is there a short quotation or precise reference in each paragraph?
Set a rule: no paragraph without evidence.
Explanation
Does the student examine the actual words?
Ask for one sentence about a single word in the quotation.
Effect
Is the reader or audience mentioned?
Give the sentence starter: "The effect on the reader is…"
Structure
Does each paragraph open with a point?
Ask for the first sentence of each paragraph to be rewritten only.
Retelling
Is the student narrating?
Ask them to cross out every sentence that only says what happens, and count what is left.
Accuracy of language
Are there errors that obscure meaning?
Mark only those. Do not mark every error in a Literature answer.

blocks.heading: Marking a class set in a reasonable time
numbered: **Read five scripts first without marking any.** You will see the pattern of the class, and the common fault will become obvious.
**Teach the common fault to the whole class**, before returning the scripts. Fifteen minutes of teaching saves thirty individual comments.
**Then mark individually, one comment each.** Because the common fault has been taught, your individual comment can address what is particular to that student.
**Keep a note of each student's one fault.** At the next piece of work, mark that first and say whether it has improved. A student who sees that you remembered takes the comment far more seriously.

blocks.title: The comment that works better than any other
text: Write a question in the margin instead of a correction: **"What effect does this have on the reader?"**, **"How do you know?"**, **"Which word tells you that?"**
A question requires an answer, and answering it is the work that produces improvement. A correction requires nothing, and usually gets nothing.

pages.title: Themes
pages.description: How to identify, express and argue a literary theme at O/L: the difference between a topic and a theme, and how to build a theme answer with evidence.
pages.keywords: literary themes, theme in literature, O/L Literature, theme essay

hero.text: A theme is not a word. It is a sentence — a claim about life that the text makes, and that you can argue about.

blocks.heading: Topic and theme are not the same thing
text: *Poverty* is a topic. *Love* is a topic. *War* is a topic. None of them can be agreed or disagreed with, and none of them can be argued for.
A **theme** is what the text says about the topic. Turn the word into a sentence and you have a theme you can write an essay about.

blocks.heading: From topic to theme
rows: Poverty
The novel shows how poverty narrows the choices of people who are otherwise capable.
Love
The play suggests that love which demands obedience is not love at all.
War
The poem presents war not as heroism but as a bureaucracy that consumes ordinary people.
Family
The story argues that families can protect and imprison a person with the same actions.
Tradition
The text suggests that tradition survives because it gives people a role, even when the role costs them.
Ambition
The play shows ambition destroying first the thing it wanted and then the person who wanted it.

blocks.heading: How to find a theme in a text

items.title: Ask what the text keeps returning to
text: A theme is not mentioned once. Look for what appears in several different places: a repeated image, a repeated situation, a question asked more than once.

items.title: Look at what characters want and cannot have
text: Themes usually live in the gap between desire and possibility. What does each main character want? What stops them? The answer to the second question is often the theme.

items.title: Look at the ending
text: What the writer chooses to reward, punish or leave unresolved tells you what the text believes. An ending that refuses to resolve is itself a statement.

items.title: Write it as a full sentence
text: Begin *The writer suggests that…* and finish the sentence. If you cannot finish it, you have a topic, not a theme.

items.title: Find three moments that support it
text: Early, middle and late in the text. Three moments across the whole text let you show development, which is what higher marks reward.

blocks.heading: Writing a theme answer
text: A theme essay goes wrong in a predictable way: the student names the theme, then retells the parts of the story where it appears. The result is a summary with a label on top.
Build it instead as an argument that develops. Each paragraph should show the theme **at a different stage** of the text and say what has changed.
numbered: **Introduction:** state the theme as a sentence, and say how the text develops it.
**Paragraph 1:** the theme as it first appears — early in the text, usually in a simple form.
**Paragraph 2:** the theme complicated — a moment where it is questioned, or where a character resists it.
**Paragraph 3:** the theme at the end — what the text finally suggests, and whether it resolves the question.
**Conclusion:** what the writer wants the reader to take away, and whether the text argues it or merely presents it.

blocks.title: A useful discipline
text: For each prescribed text, write your themes on one page as complete sentences beginning *The writer suggests that…*, with three moments listed under each.
That single page will serve almost every theme question you can be asked on that text, and it takes an hour to make.

pages.title: Characters
pages.description: How to write about literary characters at O/L: how writers reveal character, tracking change, main and minor characters, and avoiding lists of adjectives.
pages.keywords: character analysis, characterisation, O/L Literature, character development

hero.text: Characters are made of words. A character answer that never looks at the words is describing a person who does not exist.

blocks.heading: The five ways a writer reveals character
text: When you are asked how a character is *presented*, these five are what you are being asked about.
numbered: **What they say** — and how. Long speeches or short answers? Questions or orders? Do they evade?
**What they do** — especially what they do when it costs them something. A single decision reveals more than a page of description.
**What they think**, where the text gives us access. Compare it with what they say aloud; the gap is usually the point.
**What others say about them** — and whether the text shows that judgement to be fair.
**What the writer says directly** — description, and the words chosen for it. Notice whether the narrator is sympathetic, neutral or hostile.

blocks.heading: Do not write a list of adjectives
text: *He is brave, kind, honest and hardworking* is the commonest weak character answer. It is a list of labels, none of which is proved, and it would fit a hundred characters in a hundred books.

Replace each adjective with **an action and its meaning**. Instead of *he is brave*, write: *he goes back into the burning shed for the goat, although he had already been told to leave, which shows a courage that does not calculate the risk first.*
One proved quality is worth more than four asserted ones.

blocks.heading: Tracking a character across a text

items.title: Where do they begin?
text: Note their situation, their attitude, and how the writer first presents them. First impressions in literature are usually arranged deliberately.

items.title: What changes them?
text: Find the moment. Most character questions are really about this moment, whatever their wording.

items.title: What do they do differently afterwards?
text: Change must be shown in behaviour, not only stated. Find the action after the turning point that would have been impossible before it.

items.title: Where do they end?
text: Compare the last appearance with the first. This comparison, done properly, can carry an entire essay.

items.title: And if they do not change?
text: That is equally worth writing about. A character who cannot change while everyone around them does is often the point of the text.

items.definition: The central character whose choices drive the text. Not necessarily likeable, and not necessarily the narrator.
The force in opposition. It may be a person, a system, a place, or something inside the protagonist.
A character who contrasts with another and, by the contrast, shows us something about them.
items.example: A cautious brother makes a reckless one visible.

items.definition: A round character is complex and capable of surprising us; a flat one is built from a single quality. Minor characters are often flat on purpose.
A dynamic character changes; a static one does not. Both are deliberate choices by the writer.
The methods by which a writer creates a character — the five ways listed above. Use this word when the question asks *how* a character is presented.

blocks.title: Two things to avoid
bullets: **Do not judge characters as though they were your neighbours.** *She was wrong to leave her family* is a moral opinion, not literary analysis. Ask instead what the writer wants us to feel about her leaving, and how the text produces that feeling.
**Do not confuse a narrator with the author.** A first-person narrator may be mistaken, biased or lying. Asking whether you trust the narrator is often the most rewarding question you can ask.

pages.title: Literary Techniques
pages.description: The literary and dramatic techniques needed at O/L, each defined, illustrated and — most importantly — linked to the effect you must explain.
pages.keywords: literary techniques, literary devices, simile, metaphor, imagery, irony, symbolism

hero.text: Naming the technique earns one mark. Explaining what it does earns the rest. This page is mostly about the rest.

blocks.title: The three-part rule
text: Whenever you write about a technique, write three things: **name it, quote it, explain its effect.**

Most students do the first two. The mark is in the third. *The poet uses a metaphor* is not analysis; *the metaphor turns the gate's noise into a cry of pain, so the homecoming feels unwelcoming before anything has happened* is.

items.definition: A comparison using *like* or *as*.
items.example: Ask what the comparison brings with it. Comparing a crowd to a river suggests movement and force; comparing it to a herd suggests something else entirely.

items.definition: A comparison that speaks of one thing as though it were another, without *like* or *as*.
items.example: Stronger than a simile because it does not admit that it is a comparison. Ask why the writer wanted the identification to be complete.

items.definition: Giving human qualities or actions to something not human.
items.example: Ask why the writer wanted that thing to seem alive — usually to make it threatening, sympathetic, or watchful.

items.definition: Language appealing to the senses.
items.example: Never write only "the writer uses imagery". Say what kind — visual, of sound, of touch — and what the images have in common.

items.definition: An object or action standing for a larger idea.
items.example: Argue for your reading rather than assuming it. A symbol usually gathers meaning through repetition, so trace where it appears.

items.definition: Two things placed side by side so that each shows up the other.
items.example: A celebration described immediately after a funeral is not decoration; it is an argument being made by arrangement.

items.definition: Repetition of the same consonant sound at the start of nearby words.
items.example: Say what the sound does: hard consonants can suggest force or anger, soft ones calm or secrecy.

items.definition: Repetition of vowel sounds within nearby words.
items.example: Long vowels slow a line down; short ones quicken it.

items.definition: A word whose sound imitates its meaning — *crash*, *hiss*, *murmur*.
items.example: Ask whether the sounds are pleasant or harsh, and what that suggests about the scene.

items.definition: A word, phrase or structure used again deliberately.
items.example: It may suggest obsession, insistence, ritual or monotony. Say which — the word "emphasises" alone is too vague to score.

items.definition: A sentence continuing past the end of a line without a pause.
items.example: It can create speed or breathlessness, or spring a small surprise where the meaning turns at the line break.

items.definition: A strong pause within a line.
items.example: It stops the reader mid-line, often at a moment of hesitation or shock.

items.definition: How the whole text is arranged — stanzas, chapters, acts, time order.
items.example: Structural comments are highly valued and rarely made. Ask why this text is in this order.

items.definition: A contrast between what is said or expected and what is actually the case.
items.example: Distinguish verbal irony (saying the opposite of what is meant) from situational irony (an outcome opposite to what was expected).

items.definition: The audience knows something a character does not.
items.example: Say what it makes the audience feel — dread, pity, discomfort. That feeling is the effect you are being asked about.

items.definition: The attitude the writing takes to its subject.
items.example: Be precise. Not "sad", but wistful, bitter, resigned or defiant.

items.definition: The feeling created in the reader.
items.example: Tone belongs to the writer; mood belongs to the reader. Examination questions sometimes ask for one and receive the other.

items.definition: An early hint of something that comes later.
items.example: Once you know the ending, reread the opening. Foreshadowing is almost always there, and noticing it makes an answer look attentive.

items.definition: A character alone speaking their thoughts; a short remark heard only by the audience.
items.example: Both create intimacy between a character and the audience that other characters do not share.

items.definition: Deliberate exaggeration.
items.example: Ask whether it is comic, desperate or self-deceiving — exaggeration usually tells you something about the speaker.

items.definition: Deliberately saying less than is meant.
items.example: Often more powerful than exaggeration, especially about grief or fear, because the reader supplies what is left out.

blocks.heading: Practise naming and matching
intro: Naming the technique correctly is the first step. These two activities practise exactly that.

pages.title: Important Quotations
pages.description: How to choose, learn and use quotations in O/L Literature answers: why ten short quotations beat fifty long ones, and how to weave them into a sentence.
pages.keywords: quotations, quoting in literature essays, learning quotes, evidence

hero.text: Ten short quotations you can use in three different answers are worth more than fifty you can only half remember.

blocks.heading: How many, and how long
text: **Ten per text is enough.** Students who try to learn fifty end up with fifty approximate versions, and an approximate quotation is worse than none: it is an inaccuracy the examiner can see.

**Keep them short.** Between three and ten words is ideal. A long quotation eats examination time, fills your page with someone else's words rather than your analysis, and usually contains more than the point requires.

**Choose for usefulness, not for beauty.** The best quotation to learn is not the most striking line in the text; it is the one that can serve a character question, a theme question and a technique question.

items.title: One that establishes each main character
text: Usually something they say, early, that turns out to define them.

items.title: One for each main theme
text: A line where the theme is most concentrated — often a moment where a character states or refuses something.

items.title: Two from turning points
text: The moments after which nothing can go back. Almost every essay question touches one of these.

items.title: Two that show technique clearly
text: A striking image, or a piece of dialogue whose form is as revealing as its content.

items.title: One from the opening and one from the ending
text: These two together let you write about the whole shape of a text, which is worth a great deal.

blocks.heading: How to use a quotation in a sentence
text: Do not drop a quotation in on its own line and expect it to argue for you. Weave it into your own sentence so that the sentence still makes grammatical sense when read aloud.
This is called embedding, and it is one of the clearest signals of a competent Literature answer.

items.label: Compare these
sample: **Dropped in (weak):** The father is proud. "I have managed thirty years without it." This shows he is proud.
**Embedded (strong):** The father's refusal — "I have managed thirty years without it" — turns his son's offer into an occasion for measuring his own endurance.
**Embedded, shorter still:** By counting "thirty years" the father converts a simple offer into a verdict on his own life.
notes: In the weak version the quotation sits alone and does no work. The sentence before it and the sentence after it say the same thing.
In the strong version the quotation is part of the writer's own sentence, and the sentence is doing the analysis.
In the third version only two words are quoted, and they carry the whole point. Very short quotations, used precisely, are the mark of a confident answer.
Use double quotation marks, copy the words exactly, and use three dots (…) if you leave anything out of the middle.

blocks.heading: Learning them so they stay
numbered: **Write each quotation on a card, with the reason you chose it on the back** — not the meaning, the *use*: *character, pride, ch.4*.
**Say them aloud.** Quotations learnt silently are recalled approximately; quotations learnt aloud are recalled exactly.
**Test yourself backwards.** Look at the reason and recall the quotation, not the other way round. That is the direction you will need it in the examination.
**Use each one in a written sentence at least twice.** A quotation you have used is remembered; a quotation you have only read is not.
**If you cannot recall it exactly, refer to it instead.** *When the father refuses the money by counting his years* is honest and gains credit. A misquotation does not.

blocks.title: A note on this site and quotations
text: RCF English does not reproduce complete copyrighted texts. Quotations on text pages are short, accurate and used for study and criticism, with the author and work named.

**Nothing is invented.** Where a quotation cannot be verified against the text, it is not published. If you find a quotation on this site that does not match your prescribed book, please [report it](corrections/) — that is exactly the kind of error worth telling us about.

pages.title: Common Student Mistakes
pages.description: The mistakes that cost O/L Literature students the most marks — retelling the story, naming techniques without effects, unsupported claims — and how to correct each one.
pages.keywords: literature mistakes, common errors, retelling, O/L Literature, essay faults

hero.text: Ten faults account for most of the marks lost in Literature. Every one of them can be corrected in a fortnight.

blocks.heading: The ten faults, and their remedies

items.q: 1. Retelling the story instead of answering
a: **The fault:** the answer narrates events from the beginning. The examiner already knows the text.
**The test:** does each paragraph begin with a point, or with an event? If your paragraphs begin *Then he goes to…*, you are narrating.
**The remedy:** rewrite only the first sentence of each paragraph so that it makes a claim. The rest of the paragraph usually improves by itself.

items.q: 2. Naming a technique without explaining its effect
a: **The fault:** *The poet uses imagery and alliteration here.* True, and worth almost nothing.
**The remedy:** after every technique you name, write one sentence beginning **"The effect on the reader is…"** Do this every time until it becomes automatic.
**The fault:** *The mother is the strongest character in the play.* Perhaps — but why should the examiner believe you?
**The remedy:** a rule with no exceptions: **no paragraph without a short quotation or a precise reference.**
**The fault:** four lines quoted, one line of comment. Your page fills with someone else's words, and the marks are for yours.
**The remedy:** cut every quotation to ten words or fewer. If you cannot, quote two separate short pieces instead.

items.q: 5. Answering the question you prepared, not the one asked
a: **The fault:** a memorised essay on the character is delivered when the question asked about the relationship.
**The remedy:** write the question at the top of your plan and, after each paragraph, glance at it. If the paragraph does not serve the question, it is not helping you.
**The fault:** *She should not have left her husband.* This is a moral opinion about a person who does not exist.
**The remedy:** ask instead what the **writer** wants us to feel about her leaving, and which words produce that feeling.

items.q: 7. Confusing the narrator with the author
a: **The fault:** assuming that the *I* of a poem or story is the writer, and that everything the narrator says is true.
**The remedy:** ask whether the narrator can be trusted. Sometimes the gap between what the narrator believes and what the reader sees is the whole point of the text.

items.q: 8. Writing in the past tense about the text
a: **The fault:** *He went to the house and then he said…*
**The remedy:** use the present tense for what happens in a text: *He goes to the house and says…*, *the writer shows*, *the poem suggests*. Use the past only for real historical events.
**The fault:** *In this essay I am going to discuss… There are many things to say about this character.*
**The remedy:** delete the announcement and begin with your answer. Your introduction should end with a position that could be disagreed with.
**The fault:** *In conclusion, I have discussed the three points above.*
**The remedy:** a conclusion must judge. It should contain something the introduction did not — the decision you reached by writing the essay.

blocks.heading: The single most useful exercise
text: Take one of your own marked Literature answers. Cross out every sentence that only says what happens in the text.
Look at what is left. That is your actual answer, and its length usually explains your mark better than any comment written on the page.

Now rewrite one paragraph, obeying two rules: begin with a point, and include one short quotation with its effect explained. Students who do this once a week for a month generally see the difference in their next mark.

pages.title: Revision Activities
pages.description: Practical O/L Literature revision activities for students working alone or in a class, plus interactive practice on literary terms and techniques.
pages.keywords: literature revision, revision activities, O/L Literature, quiz, group revision

hero.text: Revision that only re-reads notes achieves very little. Every activity here requires you to produce something.

blocks.heading: Interactive practice
intro: Two activities on literary terms and techniques — the vocabulary you need before any analysis is possible.

blocks.heading: Activities to do on paper, alone

items.title: The one-page text summary
text: Reduce a whole text to one side of paper: one line per chapter or scene, the main characters in three words each, and three themes as full sentences. If it will not fit on one page, you do not yet know the text well enough.

items.title: Ten quotations, ten uses
text: Write your ten chosen quotations. Beside each, write the two different questions it could answer. A quotation useful for only one question is a poor choice; replace it.

items.title: The five-sentence drill
text: Take any old one-sentence answer and rewrite it in five sentences: point, evidence, explanation, effect, link. Three times a week for a fortnight.

items.title: First page, last page
text: Read the opening and the closing of a text one after the other and write a paragraph on what has changed. This exercise answers a surprising number of essay questions.

items.title: Cross out the story
text: Take a marked answer and cross out every sentence that only narrates. What remains is your real answer. Rewrite one paragraph of it properly.

items.title: Question rewriting
text: Take five past essay questions and rewrite each as a statement you could agree or disagree with. This is how you learn to see what a question is actually asking.

blocks.heading: Activities for a class or a study group

items.title: Quotation auction
text: Each student brings three quotations. The group decides which are most useful and why. Arguing about usefulness teaches selection better than being told.

items.title: Hot-seating a character
text: One student answers questions in role as a character; the rest must challenge every answer with evidence from the text. Nothing exposes shallow reading faster.

items.title: Paragraph relay
text: One student writes the point, passes it on; the next writes the evidence; the next the explanation; the next the effect. Then the group discusses the joins.

items.title: Mark a model answer
text: Give the class a deliberately average answer and ask them to mark it and justify the mark. Students who have marked once write differently afterwards.

items.title: Theme sentences
text: Give each group a topic word and ten minutes to turn it into a theme sentence supported by three moments in the text. Compare the sentences produced.

items.title: Silent scene
text: For drama: act a scene with no words, only movement and position. The class then explains what was communicated and how — which is exactly what stagecraft questions ask.

blocks.title: The last month
bullets: **Revise your own written answers, not new notes.** Your corrected work is the most efficient revision material you own.
**Write one full essay per text, timed.** One is enough if you correct it properly.
**Rewrite one weak paragraph a day.** Fifteen minutes, and it compounds.
**Recite your ten quotations aloud twice a week.** Aloud, not silently.
**Do not read a new study guide in the final fortnight.** It will make you anxious and teach you nothing you can use in time.
